title: Stages of Child Development: Prenatal and Birth to Three Years
summary: Human pregnancy lasts about 37–41 weeks; babies born before 36 weeks are preterm and after 41 weeks post-term. Conception occurs when a sperm cell combines with an egg cell to form a zygote.

Germinal stage (first two weeks after conception): about 36 hours after conception the zygote begins to divide rapidly; the ball of cells moves down the fallopian tube and, about seven days after conception, begins implantation in the uterine wall (about a week). The placenta forms — a thick, blood-rich tissue lining the wall of the uterus that passes oxygen and nutrients from the mother's blood to the embryo or foetus and removes waste.

Embryonic stage (end of the germinal stage to about 8 weeks): all the major organs form and the embryo is very fragile, about an inch long. Foetal stage (from two months after conception until birth): sex organs form, bones and muscles grow fast, the foetus moves, organ systems start to work; in the last three months the brain grows rapidly, a layer of fat forms under the skin and the respiratory and digestive systems begin to work independently.

A teratogen is any disease, drug or environmental agent that can harm the embryo or foetus — physical deformity, retarded growth or brain damage. Examples: medical and illegal drugs, alcohol and smoking (and excess nicotine or caffeine), and environmental hazards such as chemicals, radiation and extreme heat.

Umbilical cord: bluish-white; the stub dries and falls off within three weeks and becomes the belly button. Skin: wet and coated with vernix caseosa (thought to be an antibacterial barrier), greyish-blue until breathing starts. Hair: fine body hair called lanugo, which disappears within weeks. Head: very large for the body. Weight: about 2.5–3.5 kg; length grows about 2 cm a month. Sleep: newborns wake every two to three hours.

Reflexes are inborn, automatic responses: rooting (turns the head towards a touch on the cheek), sucking, palmar grasp (grasps a finger placed in the palm), Moro (thrusts arms out when support for the head and neck is suddenly removed), Babinski (fans out toes when the outer sole is stroked), startle (flings arms out at a sudden noise), eye blink (shuts eyes in bright light), stepping and swimming.

At birth infants are sensitive to light-dark contrasts and movement, prefer the human face and recognise voices. Birth–3 months: lifts and turns the head when on the stomach, kicks, grasps a toy briefly; responds to sounds by getting quiet or smiling within a few weeks; focuses on the mother's face; communicates by crying, smiles on purpose and coos by two months. 4–6 months: rolls over, better head control, sits without support by six months; grasps a rattle, transfers objects between hands; distinguishes familiar and strange faces; babbles, laughs and recognises its name.

7–10 months: crawls, pulls to stand, pincer grasp (thumb and forefinger), responds to own name and to tone of voice. 10–12 months: sits alone, pulls up, cruises along furniture, may take first steps by 12 months; finger-feeds, bangs and stacks objects; object permanence improves; imitates actions; responds to simple requests and uses gestures (shaking head for 'no', pointing, waving). As children reach their first birthday their actions become goal-oriented.

Gross motor: walks alone and backwards, picks up toys while standing, pushes and pulls, climbs on and off furniture, may begin to run. Fine motor: scribbles and paints, may prefer one hand, grasps and throws a ball, pours out contents, feeds self.

Socio-emotional: complex emotions such as jealousy, affection and shame by three; recognises self in a mirror; identifies family members; mostly plays alone or next to others (parallel play) and finds sharing hard; asserts independence by saying 'no'; attachment to the primary caregiver. Cognitive: trial-and-error experiments, mental representation, object permanence, deferred imitation, names people and objects, understands 'you' and 'me', goal-directed behaviour; thinking is concrete and attention span short.

Language: two or three words at one; one- or two-word combinations ('more cookie'), follows simple commands and points to body parts and pictures (1–2 years); between two and three, learns about 300 words, uses two- or three-word phrases, is understood by family, answers routine questions, follows two-step directions and starts using plurals, prepositions, possessives, adjectives and the past tense.

vsa: What period does infancy encompass? Write any two reflexes of infants.
Infancy is the period from birth to one year. Reflexes (any two): rooting, sucking, palmar grasp, Moro, Babinski, startle, eye blink, stepping, swimming.
What are some inherited reflexes displayed by infants at birth?
Sucking (sucks at whatever touches the lips), blinking (shuts eyes in bright light) and grasping (closes fingers on an object in the palm); also rooting, Moro, Babinski, startle and stepping.
What are infants sensitive to in terms of visual stimuli at birth?
They are sensitive to light-dark visual contrasts and to movement, and show a clear preference for gazing at the human face.
What is the sleeping pattern of newborns?

Most newborns wake every two to three hours through day and night; short stretches of sleep alternate with short periods of wakefulness, mainly for feeding and keeping dry and warm. Babies sleep about 18 hours a day.

vsa: How do drugs influence growth and development at the prenatal stage?

Drugs are teratogens: medical drugs such as some antibiotics and illegal drugs such as marijuana, opiates and cocaine can harm the foetus, causing physical deformity, retarded growth or brain damage. Alcohol and smoking slow growth and may cause mental retardation.
sa: Discuss any three characteristics of the newborn with examples.

Umbilical cord: bluish-white; the stub left after cutting dries and falls off within three weeks, becoming the belly button. Skin: wet and coated with white vernix caseosa (an antibacterial barrier), greyish-blue until breathing starts. Hair: fine body hair called lanugo on the back, shoulders and face, disappearing within weeks. Others: a large head for the body, weight of 2.5–3.5 kg, waking every two to three hours, and inborn reflexes.

or: Discuss any three milestones of language development of 2–3-year-old children.

Any three: has a word for almost everything; uses two- or three-word phrases to talk about and ask for things; is understood by family and friends; names objects to ask for them; answers routine questions ('What is your name?'); follows two-step directions ('Find your shoes and get your dress'); begins to use plurals, prepositions ('in the jar'), possessives ('mine'), adjectives and '-ed' for the past tense; enjoys simple stories, songs and rhymes.

sa: What are the two important functions of the placenta? Mention the stage of prenatal development in which it forms.

Functions: (1) it passes oxygen and nutrients from the mother's blood to the embryo or foetus, nourishing it; (2) it removes waste materials from the embryo or foetus. The placenta forms in the germinal stage (the first two weeks after conception).

or: Describe any three reflexes in a newborn.

Rooting: the infant turns the head towards anything that touches the cheek. Palmar grasp: closes the fingers and grasps an object placed in the palm. Moro: when support for the head and neck is suddenly removed, thrusts the arms out and seems to grasp. (Others: Babinski — toes fan out when the outer sole is stroked; startle; eye blink; sucking; stepping.)

sa: Describe the milestones of development of children from birth to three months.

Motor: lifts and turns the head when on the stomach by three months; stretching and kicking become vigorous; grasps a toy for a few moments. Hearing: within weeks responds to sounds by getting quiet or smiling, especially to the mother's voice. Vision: focuses on the mother's face while feeding; notices interesting sights, colours and shapes. Communication: cries to show needs, smiles on purpose, blows bubbles and coos by two months, imitates expressions and reaches for known adults for comfort.
Describe any four milestones of cognitive development of children up to three years.

Any four: object permanence — finds hidden objects; deferred imitation — imitates actions seen earlier (brushing hair, talking on a phone); trial-and-error experiments and goal-directed behaviour; names familiar people and objects and looks at the right toy when named; understands and responds to words and simple commands; distinguishes 'you' and 'me'; begins to match similar objects; pretend play with a second person.
la: Describe the stages of prenatal development and the factors that can harm the developing embryo or foetus.

Germinal stage (0–2 weeks): a sperm and egg join to form a zygote; about 36 hours later it starts dividing; the ball of cells moves to the uterus and implants about seven days after conception; the placenta forms to nourish the embryo and remove waste. Embryonic stage (to about 8 weeks): all major organs form; the embryo is fragile and about an inch long. Foetal stage (two months to birth): sex organs form, bones and muscles grow, the foetus moves, organ systems begin to function; in the last three months the brain grows fast, fat forms under the skin, and breathing and digestion start working. Harmful factors (teratogens): medical and illegal drugs; alcohol, smoking and excess caffeine, which slow growth and may cause mental retardation; and environmental hazards such as chemicals, radiation and extreme heat, which cause mutations and deformities.
Trace the milestones of development during toddlerhood (one to three years).

Physical-motor: gross — walks alone and backwards, picks up toys while standing, pushes and pulls, climbs on and off furniture, begins to run; fine — scribbles and paints, may prefer one hand, grasps and throws a ball, pours out contents, feeds self. Socio-emotional: shows fear, joy and by three complex emotions like jealousy and shame; recognises self in a mirror; identifies family; plays alone or beside others, finds sharing hard; asserts independence by saying 'no'; attached to the primary caregiver. Cognitive: object permanence, deferred imitation, trial-and-error, goal-directed behaviour, names objects, understands 'you' and 'me', short attention span. Language: from two or three words at one to about 300 words by three; two- or three-word phrases, follows simple and two-step commands, starts using plurals, possessives and the past tense.
